$comment: Budgets for the weight of this service's production dependency tree, checked by `pnpm deps:weight`.
paul-explore gained a gzipped first-load-JS budget (gpbsumido/paul-explore#396). That metric is
meaningless here — this service ships no browser bundle, so the same check would produce a number
that can go red without anything being wrong, which is worse than no check at all.
What costs a user on this service is cold start. It scales to zero — fly.toml sets
`auto_stop_machines = "stop"` and `min_machines_running = 0` — so a full boot sits on the critical
path of someone's first request. The two things that drive that boot are how much has to be
installed and paged in, and how much work happens at import time. These budgets guard the first of
those.
Say the quiet part: dependency weight is a PROXY for cold start, not cold start. paul-explore's
budget measures the bytes a browser genuinely waits on; this one measures a correlate. It is gated
anyway because it is deterministic and the thing it correlates with is not — see 'what is not
budgeted' below.
How the numbers are taken: a `pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` into a throwaway
directory, with supportedArchitectures pinned to linux/x64/glibc, then a walk of the resulting tree
deduplicating by inode so pnpm's hardlinks and symlinks are each counted once.
The architecture pin is what makes this comparable at all. sharp ships a different prebuilt libvips
per platform, so the same lockfile unpinned resolves 423.59 MiB across 331 packages on an arm64 Mac
against 441.98 MiB across 333 for the linux/x64 target — an 18 MiB swing with nothing to do with any
change under review. Pinning means the figure is identical wherever it runs and describes the machine
that actually cold starts.
`--ignore-scripts` is a known understatement, not an oversight. ffmpeg-static downloads its binary
from the network in a postinstall hook, so the real deployed image is larger than the number here by
roughly that binary. That download is not pinned by the lockfile and not reproducible offline, so
including it would trade a deterministic gate for a flaky one. This measures what the lockfile can
account for.
What is not budgeted, and why:
- Boot wall-clock. Importing the built app takes 268-294 ms on an idle laptop; on a shared CI runner
that spread is far wider. Gating on it would produce failures that re-run green, and a guard that
flakes gets ignored or deleted. Measure it by hand when it matters.
- Bundle size. There is no bundle. See above.
Raising a budget is a fine thing to do when the weight bought something. Do it in the same commit as
the dependency, so the diff shows the trade rather than just the fix.

installBytes.why: Total bytes of a production-only install, the proxy for install time and image size on a scale-to-zero boot. Measured 463,447,543 (441.98 MiB) at 4.11.3, byte-identical across repeated runs, so this leaves about 8% headroom. Note that 335 MiB of that is ffprobe-static alone, which ships prebuilt binaries for every platform in its tarball — three quarters of this budget is one dependency, and replacing it is the single change that would move this number.

packageCount.why: Number of resolved production packages including transitives, the proxy for module-resolution work at import time. Measured 333 at 4.11.3, so this leaves about 8% headroom. Counted as entries in the virtual store, so a package resolved twice at different versions counts twice — which is right, because Node pays for both.
